cards.title: Cai–Fürer–Immerman definability in choiceless polynomial time
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is the parity query for Cai–Fürer–Immerman graphs over arbitrary connected unordered base graphs definable in Choiceless Polynomial Time with counting? In the source’s construction below, is there one CPT program \(P\) that, for every finite connected base graph \(G=(V,E)\) and every \(T\subseteq V\), accepts the unordered input graph \(G^{T}\) exactly when \(|T|\) is odd?

cards.why: CFI parity is a central test of whether computation that preserves all input symmetries can match ordinary polynomial time. A negative answer would separate CPT with counting from polynomial time; a positive answer would remove an important candidate obstruction without by itself proving that CPT captures every polynomial-time property.
cards.status_note: Read the full primary CPT definition and exact CFI construction, the later hypercube nondefinability statement and restricted XOR-circuit theorem, and the 2025 symmetric-IPS model comparison. Searched through 12 September 2026 without finding a full resolution. The 2024 arXiv hypercube upload is a copy of a 2021 conference paper. The original 1999 separation for a version without counting is not a separation for this counting model. The 2023 paper’s extra edge-gadget pairing is not silently inserted into the primary-source construction.

progress.text: The source extends positive results to additional base-graph classes and retains the arbitrary unordered case.
A lower bound for constructing fine preorders on hypercubes limits one known approach.
Symmetric XOR-circuits provide partial lower-bound connections, with additional hypotheses and a remaining gap.
Symmetric algebraic proof results further connect these models without settling full CPT parity definability.

sentences: CFI graphs hide an even-or-odd parity in symmetric gadgets built over a base graph.
The input provides adjacency but no arbitrary order or labels revealing the hidden parity.
The question asks for one choiceless polynomial-time program with counting that recovers parity for every base graph.
The model may construct nested sets, but its total resources are polynomial in the expanded input size.
Known positive cases and restricted lower bounds do not settle the full unordered question.

references.title: Definability of Cai-Fürer-Immerman Problems in Choiceless Polynomial Time
references.authors: Pakusa, Wied; Schalthöfer, Svenja; Selman, Erkal
references.locator: Explicit open question on PDF page 3

cards.definitions:
The base graph is finite, nonempty, simple and undirected. Write \(E(v)\) for the edges incident with \(v\). Use the vertex-parity construction of Section 3 of the primary source. For each base edge \(e\), introduce two distinct vertices \(e_{0},e_{1}\). For each base vertex \(v\), introduce a vertex \(v^{X}\) for every subset \(X\subseteq E(v)\) satisfying
\[|X|\equiv\mathbf1_{v\in T}\pmod2.\]
For each such \(v^{X}\) and each \(e\in E(v)\), join \(v^{X}\) to \(e_{1}\) if \(e\in X\), and to \(e_{0}\) otherwise. These are all the edges in this primary-source convention. Thus an even gadget uses even subsets, and an odd gadget uses odd subsets.

The constructed names describe the mathematical construction; they are not readable labels in the input. The program receives only an unordered graph isomorphic to \(G^{T}\), through its adjacency relation. It receives no order of base vertices, no designation of which edge-gadget vertex is 0 or 1, no set \(T\), and no list of the subsets \(X\). There is no auxiliary coloring, padding or supplied circuit. The source’s parity query distinguishes the two CFI types over each connected base graph. Inputs outside the promised CFI family need not be recognized.

The resource parameter is \(N=|V(G^{T})|\), the size of the explicit expanded input, not \(|V(G)|\). A high-degree base vertex can generate exponentially many gadget vertices. The program and its polynomial resource bound must work uniformly over all base graphs and all twists \(T\).

CPT here includes counting. Its data domain consists of the input vertices as indivisible atoms and hereditarily finite sets built from these atoms: finite sets whose members are atoms or further such finite sets, with finite nesting depth. The available constants include the empty set and the set of all atoms. Operations are unordered pairing \(\{x,y\}\), union, extracting the unique member of a singleton (returning the empty set otherwise), and cardinality. Cardinalities are encoded as von Neumann ordinals, where \(0=\varnothing\) and \(m+1=m\cup\{m\}\). Counting an atom returns the empty set.

Terms are built from variables, these constants and operations, and bounded set comprehensions
\[\{s(\bar x,y):y\in r(\bar x)\text{ and }\varphi(\bar x,y)\}.\]
Tests use equality, membership and input adjacency, combined by Boolean connectives. Comprehensions range over an already constructed finite set; there is no primitive that arbitrarily chooses a member of a non-singleton set or provides an order on the atoms.

A program is fixed finite syntax for a state-update term and two tests, for halting and acceptance. Beginning with empty state, it repeatedly applies the update and checks the tests. There is a fixed polynomial bound in \(N+1\) on the number of iterations and on the number of distinct objects in the transitive closures of the states. A transitive closure includes all recursively nested members, so a huge set cannot be hidden inside a small outer container. Exceeding a bound aborts and rejects. Equivalent standard encodings of the CPT formalism give the same definability question.

All permitted operations respect permutations of the input atoms that preserve adjacency. Numerical ordinals can be ordered, but this does not authorize an arbitrary order of graph vertices. The question permits unbounded finite nesting depth subject to the polynomial size bound; it is not limited to fixed-rank sets or tuples.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one CPT program with counting and prove its polynomial resource bound and correct parity decision on every promised unordered CFI input, or prove no such program exists. A negative result for a restricted family of CPT programs, or failure to construct a particular auxiliary order, does not establish nondefinability in full CPT.

context_blocks.title: Ordinary polynomial-time solvability is already known
context_blocks.text: The source presents the parity query as a polynomial-time problem whose status in full choiceless computation is unknown. Merely giving an ordinary algorithm that uses arbitrary vertex choices would not answer the definability question.

context_blocks.title: Order and input size explain the positive special cases
context_blocks.text: The primary paper gives CPT procedures when the base graph has a supplied preorder with logarithmically sized color classes, and when its maximum degree is linear in its size. In the latter case the expanded CFI graph is exponentially larger than the base graph. Neither theorem covers arbitrary unordered bounded-degree bases.

context_blocks.title: Known lower bounds restrict the model or an auxiliary task
context_blocks.text: The primary paper proves limitations for computation without set-like objects. Pago’s CSL 2021 paper shows that sufficiently fine preorders cannot be constructed on all hypercubes; this blocks a particular strategy rather than deciding the parity query’s expressibility. The 2023 XOR-circuit result imposes additional conditions on CPT programs and explicitly retains a gap in its circuit lower-bound argument.

context_blocks.title: Later symmetric proof bounds are a different result
context_blocks.text: The 2025 paper connects CPT with symmetric algebraic proofs and gives polynomial-size symmetric IPS proofs for CFI-related equations. An existence or simulation theorem for those proofs does not supply a uniform CPT parity algorithm. The paper continues to treat full CPT with counting as a candidate for capturing polynomial time.

cards.context:
The source presents the parity query as a polynomial-time problem whose status in full choiceless computation is unknown. Merely giving an ordinary algorithm that uses arbitrary vertex choices would not answer the definability question.

The primary paper gives CPT procedures when the base graph has a supplied preorder with logarithmically sized color classes, and when its maximum degree is linear in its size. In the latter case the expanded CFI graph is exponentially larger than the base graph. Neither theorem covers arbitrary unordered bounded-degree bases.

The primary paper proves limitations for computation without set-like objects. Pago’s CSL 2021 paper shows that sufficiently fine preorders cannot be constructed on all hypercubes; this blocks a particular strategy rather than deciding the parity query’s expressibility. The 2023 XOR-circuit result imposes additional conditions on CPT programs and explicitly retains a gap in its circuit lower-bound argument.

The 2025 paper connects CPT with symmetric algebraic proofs and gives polynomial-size symmetric IPS proofs for CFI-related equations. An existence or simulation theorem for those proofs does not supply a uniform CPT parity algorithm. The paper continues to treat full CPT with counting as a candidate for capturing polynomial time.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
